Stimulation of methane yield rate from food waste by aerobic pre-treatment
Chuanfu Wua,b,1, Miao Yua,1, Qiqi Huanga, Hongzhi Maa, Ming Gaoa,b,⁎, Qunhui Wanga,b,
Kenji Sakaic
a Department of Environmental Engineering, School of Energy and Environmental Engineering, University of Science and Technology Beijing, 30 Xueyuan Road, Haidian
District, Beijing 100083, China
b Beijing Key Laboratory on Resource-oriented Treatment of Industrial Pollutants, University of Science and Technology Beijing, 30 Xueyuan Road, Haidian District, Beijing
10083, China
c Department of Bioscience and Biotechnology, Faculty of Agriculture Graduate School, Kyushu University, 6-10-1 Hakozaki, Higashi-ku, Fukuoka 812-8581, Japan
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Food waste
Aerobic pre-treatment
Anaerobic digestion
Methane yield rate
COD loss
A B S T R A C T
Aerobic pre-treatment (AP) was applied to enhance methane yield from food waste through anaerobic digestion.
Diﬀerent AP durations (i.e. 2, 5 and 8 days) prior to anaerobic digestion were tested. The results indicated that
AP of food waste led to no signiﬁcant diﬀerences (p > 0.05) in methane yield potential (ca. 418 mL/g-VS).
However, a suitable AP duration (5 days) increased methane yield rates (ca. 18 mL/d/g-VS; 22.0% higher than
the control) by anticipating methane generation and shortening the methanogenic phase via volatile fatty acid
reduction and pH increase. Although AP induced chemical oxygen demand loss to some extent (i.e. by
2.6%–9.9%) in the AP stage via aerobic degradation, the methane yield potential could be recovered by en-
hancing organic matter hydrolysis. Therefore, maximisation of hydrolysis should be used as a basis for de-
termining a suitable AP duration for various types of organic matter.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is one of the most attractive methods used
for the disposal of food waste (FW) in China owing to its potential for
producing biogas and the fact that the use of anaerobic digesters is
economical (Wu et al., 2015a,b, 2018; Kawai et al., 2014; Liu et al.,
2013; Kim and Kim, 2013). According to literature, more than 70% of
demonstration projects for FW disposal in China employ methane fer-
mentation technology (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2015). Therefore, the
development of technology that stimulates methane yield from FW is of
great signiﬁcance.
In AD, organic matter is converted into methane by three speciﬁc
bacterial groups: (i) fermentative bacteria, which hydrolyse polymers
into acetic acid and other organic acids, along with hydrogen and
carbon dioxide; (ii) hydrogen-producing bacteria, which convert pro-
pionate and higher fatty acids produced by the fermentative bacteria
into acetate and hydrogen and (iii) methanogenic bacteria, which
produce methane from acetate and/or hydrogen and carbon dioxide
(Mshandete et al., 2005). However, when treating a particulate per-
ishable substrate, e.g. FW, which is rich in carbohydrate and protein
(Yu et al., 2018; Raﬁeenia et al., 2017), the maintenance of the balance
between ‘acid-forming’ and ‘methane-generating’ microorganisms is
diﬃcult in traditional single-stage AD systems. This leads to the accu-
mulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs), acidiﬁcation, disruption of the
stability of the AD system and low methane yields (Wu et al., 2015b,
2018; Kawai et al., 2014). Therefore, the prevention of acidiﬁcation is a
key to ensuring stable and high-eﬃciency operation of AD systems.
Given that acidiﬁcation of AD systems is caused by VFA accumu-
lation (resulting in a reduction in pH of the fermentation digestate) and
an imbalance between ‘acid-forming’ and ‘acid-consuming’ bacterial
groups, multiple countermeasures have been developed. One such ap-
proach entails increasing the alkalinity/pH of the fermentation diges-
tate (Liew et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2010) and preventing the suppression
of methanogenic bacteria caused by low pH. An alternative approach is
to alleviate the ‘burden’ of the unit cell of methanogenic bacteria by
decreasing the organic loading, reducing its perishable nature by
mixing it with persistent materials (e.g. lignocellulosic material) and
increasing the inoculum donation (i.e. methanogenic bacteria) (Wu
et al., 2018; Ebner et al., 2014; Lű et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
However, these countermeasures may, to some extent, decrease volu-
metric eﬃciency and increase the operating costs of AD systems (Jiang
et al., 2012). A further strategy in addition to a robust improvement in
the methanogenic bacteria population by regulating the growth en-

adjustment) is directing the acidogenic metabolites towards ethanol
instead of VFAs; this is achieved by adding yeast to the FW during the
pre-treatment stage (Yu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2016; Wu et al.,
2015b). Nevertheless, the mechanisms and ﬁeld applicability of this
technology require further study prior to its wide implementation.
To maintain the balance between hydrolytic and methanogenic re-
actions and reduce the retardation of methanogenic bacteria growth
caused by the accumulation of VFAs, the strategy of aerobic pre-treat-
ment (AP) of the organic matter prior to AD has been developed in
recent years. In this AD scenario, organic acids generated from the
organic matter hydrolysis process can be quickly decomposed. This
increases the pH of the fermentative substrate, subsequently improving
the start-up stability of the AD system and quickly establishing the
methanogenic phase (Raﬁeenia et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2014, 2016).
Moreover, organic matter hydrolysis, which is considered as the rate-
limiting step in AD, can be promoted under aerobic conditions, likely
because of the greater production of enzymes (Raﬁeenia et al., 2017;
Peces et al., 2016; Cossu et al., 2016; Charles et al., 2009). However,
inappropriate AP strategies might reduce the methane production po-
tential owing to the loss of organic matter (Xu et al., 2014, 2016; Cossu
et al., 2016; Gerassimidou et al., 2013; Brummeler and Koster, 1990).
To maximise biogas recovery from organic matter, numerous studies
have optimised AP conditions such as aeration rates (e.g. 0.7–32.0 NL/
d/kgTS; Cossu et al., 2016), frequencies (e.g. continuous/intermittent
aeration and gradually reduced aeration; Xu et al., 2016; Cossu et al.,
2016; Sang et al., 2009), duration (varying from hours to months; Cossu
et al., 2016; Gerassimidou et al., 2013; Mshandete et al., 2005; Zach
et al., 2000) and temperature (e.g. mesophilic and thermophilic; Peces
et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2014; Hasegawa et al., 2000). The inﬂuence of
AP on biogas production varies according to the characteristics of the
organic matter with both positive and negative impacts documented in
the studies mentioned above. Formulation of the AP parameters based
on MSW properties is diﬃcult because of the heterogeneous nature of
MSW. In addition, although indexes of pH, total VFAs (TVFA) and
oxygen consumption have been used to determine the aeration duration
(Xu et al., 2016; Cossu et al., 2016), ﬁnding a suitable speciﬁc chemical
parameter that is applicable and capable of guaranteeing optimal
conditions for mathanogenic bacteria is still a challenge.
An in-depth understanding of the inﬂuence of AP on organic matter
fermentation processes, including both hydrolytic and methanogenic
processes, is fundamentally important for improving the eﬃciency of
AP. This study aims to evaluate the eﬀects of AP duration on the me-
thane yield rate of FW by examining the characteristic parameters as-
sociated with methane generation (i.e. methane yield rate, hydrolysis
degree, cumulative volume produced, lag time and chemical oxygen
demand (COD) reduction). This analysis will be useful for identifying
the optimum AP strategy for stimulating methane production. The re-
sults thus obtained may lay the foundation for the optimal design of
AP–AD systems and provide a scientiﬁc basis for further study.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
The FW used in this study was collected from the cafeteria of a dining
hall at the University of Science and Technology Beijing, China. The
constituents of the FW were highly irregular, comprising mainly grain,
vegetables and small amounts of meat and ﬁsh. Polyvinyl resins, egg shells
and animal bones were removed before the FW was crushed in a blender
(< 5-mm particle size). The FW slurry was stored at −20 °C to prevent
deterioration. Anaerobic digester sludge for use as seed sludge was ob-
tained from sedimentation tanks in the Xiaojiahe sewage treatment plant.
The anaerobic digester sludge was subjected to acclimatisation for two
months before the experiments. The accommodation methodology can be
found elsewhere (Wu et al., 2015). The chemical characteristics of the
fermentation substrate and inoculum are shown in Table 1.
2.2. Experimental system
Screening for the optimum AP time and the eﬀect of inoculum-to-
substrate ratio (ISR) on methane yield were conducted in wide-
mouthed 500-mL Erlenmeyer ﬂasks. Each fermentation bioreactor was
sealed with a gas-tight rubber stopper and the bioreactor had an outlet
equipped with a sampling septum for taking biogas samples, a 1000-mL
gas-tight bag for biogas collection and a discharge outlet at the bottom
with a switch to collect the fermentation digestate. The study entailed
two experiments.
2.2.1. Experiment 1: screening for optimum AP duration
To examine the eﬀect of AP duration on the subsequent perfor-
mance of the batch AD of FW, AP experiments were conducted over
three diﬀerent durations: 2, 5 and 8 days (hereafter referred to as AP-2,
AP-5 and AP-8, respectively). In this experiment, 71.2 g of FW slurry
were added to the 500-mL Erlenmeyer ﬂasks under aerobic conditions
(maintained by leaving the ﬂasks open to the environment). During the
AP, the ﬂasks were agitated three times per day, and distilled water was
added to each ﬂask to compensate for water evaporation, thus main-
taining the original substrate weight. The AP experiments were con-
ducted at a temperature of 37 ± 1 °C. Immediately after the AP step (2,
5 or 8 d), the ﬂasks were ﬁlled with 350-mL acclimatised anaerobic
digester sludge, corresponding to an ISR of 1.0 g-VSinoculum/g-VSFW.
Subsequently, the ﬂasks were ﬂushed with nitrogen gas for 10 min to
create anaerobic conditions for AD. Methane fermentation was con-
ducted at 37 ± 1 °C, and mixing was performed at 50 rpm using an air-
bath rotary shaker. In addition, a control methane fermentation treat-
ment was prepared by mixing FW slurry and acclimatised anaerobic
digester sludge (ISR 1.0) without AP. Two ﬂasks containing only the
inoculum were prepared as blanks, and the methane yield of these
blanks was deducted from each treatment. The biogas production of
each treatment was quantiﬁed daily, and indexes of the fermentation
digestate were assayed every alternate day.
2.2.2. Experiment 2: eﬀect of ISR on methane yield from FW that had
previously been aerobically pre-treated
This experiment was performed to investigate the eﬀect of ISR on
the methane yield of FW subjected to AP. In this experiment, 78.2 g of
FW slurry (instead of 71.2 g FW slurry) were subjected to AP for 5 days
in Erlenmeyer ﬂasks. The ﬂasks were then ﬁlled with 350-mL accli-
matised anaerobic digester sludge (corresponding to an ISR of 0.9 g-
VSinoculum/g-VSFW), and anaerobic conditions were created by ﬂushing
with nitrogen gas prior to the subsequent AD experiment. The experi-
mental conditions of the AD were the same as those described above.
All the digestion experiments were conducted in duplicate with the
average of the duplicates presented herein.

2.3. Analytical methods
The total solid (TS) and volatile solid (VS) were measured by weight
loss at 105 °C and 560 °C, respectively. The carbon and nitrogen con-
tents of the solid samples were measured using a CNH analyser (J-
SCIENCE LAB Co., Japan). Values of pH were recorded using a PHS-3C
type digital acidometer. Both VFAs and ethanol were measured via
high-performance liquid chromatography following the method re-
ported by Yu et al. (2018). The alkalinity of liquid samples was quan-
tiﬁed by titration using bromocresol green–methyl red as an indicator.
The daily methane yields of the bottles were calculated based on the gas
generation amounts (collected by the gas sampling bags) and the me-
thane contents in the biogas samples. The methane contents were
analysed via gas chromatography (GC-2010, Shimadzu International
Trading Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) equipped with a CP-Porabond Q
column and a thermal conductivity detector. The daily methane yield of
each treatment was converted to the corresponding volume at standard
temperature (273.15 K) and pressure (1 atm).
To mathematically simulate the cumulative methane yield of each
treatment, a modiﬁed Gompertz growth equation was adopted. The
model is characterised as having a sigmoidal shape with a clear in-
ﬂection point (Cossu et al., 2016; Sandip et al., 2012). The equation is

3. Results
3.1. Methane yield of FW
The main results of the batch AD of FW following diﬀerent AP
durations are shown in terms of cumulative methane yield in Fig. 1. The
cumulative methane yield ranged between 357.5 and 442.8 mL/g-VS
after 31 days of digestion in all treatments. The highest methane yields
recorded for ISR 1.0 were 417.3–418.6 mL/g-VS for AP-5 and the
control group, followed by the yields of 392.9 and 357.7 mL/g-VS for
AP-2 and AP-8, respectively. The methane yield of AP-5 at ISP 0.9 was
442.8 mL/g-VS. Notably, the methane yields over the ﬁrst 24 days of
fermentation (the methane yield cut-oﬀpoint for AP-5 and AP-8) for
AP-5 (ISR 1.0 and 0.9) were signiﬁcantly (p < 0.05) higher than those
of AP-2, AP-8 and the control group. The average methane yield rate of
AP-5 (ISR 1.0 and 0.9) ranged from 17.3 to 18.5 mL/d/g-VS, which was
approximately 18.6%, 18.4% and 22.0% higher than that of AP-2, AP-8
and the control group, respectively.
Table 2 showed the methane yield potential, maximal daily me-
thane yield and lag time of diﬀerent treatments. Statistical indicators
(R2) were used to evaluate the reliability of the kinetic model results.
The R2 values of the treatments ranged from 0.994 to 0.998, indicating
that the modiﬁed Gompertz equation is suitable to model biogas pro-
duction during the test. As shown in Table 2, the ﬁtted methane yield
potentials of FW in diﬀerent treatments were basically consistent to the
measured methane yield potential. Additionally, the shortest methane
yield lag times were 0.6 d for AP-5 (ISR 1.0), followed by 1.2, 1.6, 1.7
and 2.7 d for AP-5 (ISR 0.9), AP-2, AP-8 and the control group, re-
spectively. The results revealed that suitable AP prior to AD could not
only preserve the methane generation potential of the FW and improve
the organic matter treatment capacity of the AD system but also pro-
mote the methane yield rate by shortening the methane yield lag time
(compared with conventional AD systems).
3.2. Volatile fatty acid, ethanol, pH and alkalinity
Methane yield and organic matter treatment capacity depend
mainly on operational parameters such as organic loading rate (OLR),
pH and temperature (Wu et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2010). In particular,
the evolution of VFAs plays an important role in maintaining an eﬃ-
cient AD as it strongly aﬀects the pH, alkalinity and activity of me-
thanogens (Wu et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2010). Fig. 2 shows the changes
in VFAs, ethanol, pH and alkalinity in the methanogenic reactors. In all
treatments, TVFAs accumulated and reached their highest level on Day
4, decreasing thereafter. The TVFA concentrations were higher in AP-2
and the control group in the ﬁrst 12 days of methanogenic fermenta-
tion. This is attributed to the low VFA consumption rates in these two
treatments and is in accord with the methane yield trend observed in
Fig. 1. Previous studies have suggested that a TVFA concentration >
6 g/L may result in a reduction in biogas production, whereas a
value > 8 g/L may strongly inhibit AD (Karthikeyan and Visvanathan,
2013; Siegert and Banks, 2005). On this basis, AP-5 (ISR 1.0 and 0.9)
and AP-8 tended to alleviate the inhibition caused by TVFAs at the
beginning of fermentation (i.e. the TVFA concentration was lower than
6 g/L over the ﬁrst 10 d) and consequently may have reduced the lag
time, in line with the trend observed in Table 2.
In addition to the concentration of VFAs, their composition in the
fermentation digestate may aﬀect AD performance; this is a critical
index reﬂecting the status of the AD system. Generally, there are two
common pathways for the acidogenic fermentation of organic matter
(i.e. propionic and butyric acid fermentation pathways), with acetic
acid, propionic acid and butyric acid as the dominant VFAs (Zhu et al.,
2010; Ren et al., 1995). The ﬁndings of our study showed concurrence
with the expected results. It is obvious that appreciable accumulations
of propionic and butyric acids were found in all treatments (Fig. 2). This
observation may be accounted for as follows. First, there is a lack of
propionate- and butyric-degrading syntrophic acetogenic bacteria,
which are capable of transforming propionic and butyric acids to acetic
acid, in the inoculum. Second, a large fraction of propionic and butyric
acids was detected during the AD process, suggesting that the system
became overloaded under the prevalent ISR condition (Kawai et al.,
2014). A previous study demonstrated that an ISR of 1.0 is critical for
the AD of FW (Wu et al., 2015). The results of this study suggest that the
ISR can be further reduced to 0.9 when AP-5 is adopted, as evidenced
by the methane yield of the AP-5 treatment (Fig. 1).
System pH is an important parameter for proper operation and
monitoring of the AD process as it may aﬀect acidogenic fermentation
and the activity of methanogens (Wu et al., 2018; Ren et al., 1995). The
pH of the fermentation digestate depends strongly on the buﬀering
capacity, VFA presence and alkalinity of the AD system (Hernandez and
Rodriguez, 2013; Zhu et al., 2010). As shown in Fig. 2, pH initially
decreased with an increase in VFA production by acidogenic bacteria

nearly 6.5 was observed in all treatments (except for AP-5 (ISR 1.0), for
which the lowest pH was 6.7). Alkalinity showed a similar trend to pH.
The increases in pH and alkalinity during the later stage could be owing
to the consumption of VFAs by the methanogens. Notably, pH recovery
(increase) in the AP-5 (ISR 1.0 and 0.9) and AP-8 treatments was faster
than that in the other treatments. This is likely attributable to the re-
latively high pH of the fermentation digestate at the very beginning of
AD (the initial pH values of the fermentation digestate were 7.9, 8.1,
8.2, 7.8 and 7.8 for AP-2, AP-5 (ISR 1.0), AP-8, the control group and
AP-5 (ISR 0.9), respectively). These results indicate that suitable AP
might increase the pH, and consequently the stabilisation, of the AD
system via the improvement of initial digestate quality (i.e. low TVFA
levels and high pH).

system process, its stimulation may lead to more rapid AD. The hy-

treatment at diﬀerent stages is shown in Table 3. The highest total

(ISP 0.9), respectively. It is noteworthy that most of the organic matter
was hydrolysed during the methanogenic stage, which is consistent

increase in AP duration improved the hydrolysis degree in the pre-
treatment stage. The hydrolysis degree in the methanogenic stage was
higher than 75% in all treatments except AP-5 (ISP 0.9). Previous re-
search has demonstrated that an organic matter hydrolysis degree
of > 75% in the methanogenic stage is crucial for maintaining the
stability of AD systems (Wu et al., 2018). From this standpoint, dis-
regarding its methane yield, the stability of the AD system in a con-
tinuous feed mode with AP-5 (ISP 0.9) still needs to be assessed. The
average daily hydrolysis rate was greatest for AP-5 (ISP 1.0). Although
the total hydrolysis degree of organic matter was large in AP-8, the
average daily hydrolysis rate was low compared with other treatments.
These results suggest that suitable AP can to some extent improve both
the total hydrolysis degree and average daily hydrolysis rate.
4. Discussion
4.1. Relation between daily methane yield and process parameters
Given its high biodegradability, the irreversible acidiﬁcation of the
digestate (resulting from rapid hydrolysis and acidogenesis) is a major
challenge to the AD of FW as it can inhibit methanogenesis and cause
failure of the digestion process (Zhu et al., 2010). As an eﬀective
countermeasure, AP has been used as a means of increasing the pH of
the digestate via degradation of VFAs. Moreover, AP can encourage the
hydrolysis of organic matter and consequently improve the quality of
the discharged fermentation digestate. The positive impact of AP on the
AD of organic matter in this study is comparable with those ﬁndings
listed in Table 4. However, inappropriate AP strategies (primarily an
unsuitable AP duration) might lead to over-consumption of VFAs, re-
sulting in a reduction of the methane production potential. In addition,
inappropriate AP strategies might oﬀer little advantage in terms of
improving organic matter hydrolysis (as shown in Table 3). Therefore,
for a speciﬁc type of organic matter, the identiﬁcation of a suitable AP
that allows for (i) stimulation of the methane yield rate of the organic
matter and (ii) recovery of organic carbon loss via promotion of the
hydrolysis degree is vital.
To ascertain the optimum AP strategy, it is necessary to unravel the
correlation between daily methane yield and the various process
parameters. Based on Table 5, daily methane yield has the strongest
positive linear correlation with pH of the digestate. Therefore, suitable
AP might increase methane yield via an increase in the pH of the di-
gestate in the initial fermentation stage. Previous research has de-
monstrated that the inhibition of methanogenesis by acidiﬁcation might
contribute to a decrease in pH to undesirable levels, instead of VFAs
accumulation, since short-chain VFAs are not toxic (Kwietniewska and
Tys, 2014). Moreover, it is reported that the complete recoverable yield
of methane from FW should be > 400 mL/g-VS in a stable running AD
system (Kawai et al., 2014), resulting in a daily methane yield of >
13.3 mL/g-VS when the HRT of the organic matter is assumed to be 30
d. The results herein suggest that the complete recoverable yield of
methane can be obtained at pH > 7.5 (Fig. 3), which is consistent with
previous studies (Wu et al., 2018; Kawai et al., 2014). In addition,
correlation analysis results suggested that the reduction of pH in the
fermentation digestate was partially owing to the accumulation of
TVFAs, acetic acid and butyric acid, indicating that the high organic
loading (i.e. butyric acid accumulation) may have aﬀected the activity
of the acetic acid-consuming bacteria (i.e. methanogenesis). This was
also demonstrated by the result that butyric acid had the second
strongest positive linear correlation with daily methane yield (Table 5).
Therefore, the rapid establishment (i.e. short lag time) of methano-
genesis fermentation observed during the AP might have also been
assisted by the reduction in TVFA levels at the beginning of AD (Fig. 2).

A previous study has demonstrated that the daily methane yield of
AD systems is aﬀected by the levels of propionic acid, propionic acid/
acetic acid, alkalinity and TVFA/ alkalinity (Wu et al., 2015). Propionic
acid is generated owing to microbial regulation of the NADH/NAD+
balance during acetic acid generation, even in a stable AD process (Ren
et al., 1995). The presence of low propionic acid levels might indicate
either an insuﬃcient digestion substrate for methanogens (inhibition of
acetogenic bacteria) or that the AD system was highly functional (i.e.
propionic acid was rapidly converted into acetic acid), whereas high
propionic acid levels might suggest a disorder in the acetogenic and/or
methanogenic processes. Therefore, relying solely on the propionic acid
level to predict AD performance is not prudent. Recently, the ratio of
propionic acid/acetic acid has been considered a suitable early index
for predicting the inhibition or stability of AD systems; a ratio ranging
from 0.03 to 0.1 is optimal for methane yield whereas a value of > 1.4
is representative of digester failure (Wu et al., 2015; Kwietniewska and
Tys, 2014). However, the results of the present study diﬀer from those
obtained previously. The daily methane yield herein showed a positive
linear correlation with both propionic acid and the propionic acid/
acetic acid ratio. The highest propionic acid/acetic acid ratio found in
this study was nearly 6.0, which is far larger than the values observed in
the studies mentioned above. This may be attributable to the fact that
the short-chain VFAs are not toxic and their inhibition eﬀects are
mostly contributed by the reduction in pH. The pH of the digestate
was > 7.0 in all treatments; this is optimal for methanogens (i.e.
pH = 7–8; Angelidaki and Sanders, 2004). Therefore, the proper con-
trol of pH in AD systems is of great importance.
The pH of the digestate in the AD system had strong positive linear
correlation with alkalinity (Table 5). The results herein suggest that a
daily methane yield of > 13.3 mL/g-VS (i.e. the complete recoverable
yield) can be obtained when alkalinity is > 10, which is consistent with
previous research (Wu et al., 2018). In contrast, alkalinity can be used
to reduce the risk of over-loading AD systems via the control of the
TVFA/ alkalinity ratio. It is reported that a digester can run stably at a
TVFA/alkalinity ratio of < 0.4 (Gallaghan et al., 2002), 0.8 (Farquhar
and Rovers, 1973) and even 1.25 (Cossu, et al., 2016); however, it has
also been reported that it becomes unstable in range 0.4–0.8 (Gallaghan
et al., 2002). The results of this study indicate that a satisfactory TVFA/
alkalinity ratio was in the range 0.2–0.8 (deﬁned in terms of a daily
methane yield of > 13.3 mL/g-VS) and was optimum at 0.5 (Fig. 3).
Higher or lower TVFA/alkalinity ratios might produce a negative eﬀect
on methane yield owing to insuﬃcient substrate or poor environmental
conditions for methanogens (i.e. low alkalinity and pH and over-
feeding).
4.2. Inﬂuence of AP strategies on COD mass balance
In the light of the above-mentioned results, the promotion of me-
thane yield from FW can be attributed to pH/alkalinity increases due to
the aerobic decomposition of VFAs. However, the mechanism relating
to the eﬀect of diﬀerent AP durations on AD is still unclear. To elucidate
changes in methane-forming material during AD, the COD mass balance
of the diﬀerent treatments was investigated. As shown in Table 6, COD
loss of the substrate was larger in the AP treatment than in the control
group. Moreover, a longer AP duration induced higher COD loss at a
speciﬁc ISR (i.e. ISR = 1.0). Notably, extensive AP (i.e. AP-8) induced

higher COD losses in both the pre-treatment and methanogenic stages.
This may have contributed to the low methane yield observed in AP-8.
Conversely, although a suitable AP strategy (i.e. AP-5 (ISR 1.0)) led to
moderate COD loss, the methane production potential could be re-
covered by the promotion of the hydrolysis degree of the organic matter
(Table 6). The methane yield rates per gram of COD were lower than
the theoretical value (i.e. 1 g-COD = 350 mL methane) in all treatments
owing to COD loss during AD. However, the theoretical methane yield
rate per gram of COD (i.e. the COD loss during AD converted into
methane yield) was close to the theoretical value and AP-5 (ISR 1.0)
could even enhance the methane yield of the inoculum (deﬁned in
terms of the coeﬃcient of 364.7 mL/g-COD). These ﬁndings are likely
due to the following: (i) after suitable AP, the switch from aerobic to
anaerobic conditions renders the transition from an aerobic to an
anaerobic microbial population more dynamic (Cossu, et al., 2016;
Jang et al., 2014) and (ii) the increased synergism among microbial
species, by improving the hydrolysis of the rate-limiting step with the
help of AP, might be beneﬁcial for the methane production (Peces et al.,
2016; Jang et al., 2014). In addition, although the increased OLR (i.e.
low ISR) led to low COD loss (i.e. AP-5 (ISR 0.9)), it may increase the
diﬃculty of fermentation digestate disposal (due to the high level of
organic matter remaining). Regardless, the volumetric methane yield
rate of the FW in AP-5 was the highest of all the treatments (Table 6),
indicating the potential usefulness of the strategy.
5. Conclusions
Diﬀerent AP durations were tested prior to AD. Although AP-5
showed no signiﬁcant diﬀerence (p > 0.05) in methane yield potential
compared with the control group, it stimulated the methane yield rate
by anticipating methane generation and shortening the methanogenic
phase resulting from VFA reduction and pH increase. Notably, although
AP induced COD loss to some extent in the AP stage (2.6%–9.9%), the
methane yield potential could be recovered by an increase in organic
matter hydrolysis. Therefore, maximisation of the hydrolysis should be
used as the basis for determining the optimum AP duration for speciﬁc
organic matter types.
